question: Why doesn't solid material, when it breaks simply connect back together? What kept it together that is gone now?
answer_raw:
Nothing mysterious disappears. The atoms were held together by chemical bonds, and those bonds only work over extremely short distances, roughly the width of an atom or two. When you push two broken pieces back together, they seem to fit perfectly, but at the atomic scale the surfaces are jagged, slightly deformed, and misaligned. Only a tiny fraction of atoms end up close enough to rebond.

There's a second problem. The instant a fresh surface forms, it reacts with the air. Metals grow oxide layers, and nearly everything picks up a film of water and gas molecules. That contamination sits between the surfaces and blocks new bonds.

Remove both obstacles and materials really do rejoin. Clean, flat metal pieces touching in a vacuum can "cold weld" together, which is a real headache for spacecraft engineers.

question: How is it that rich kids in can get into the best and presumably most exclusive (e.g. Ivy League) colleges, despite having average or poor grades in high school?
answer_raw:
Mostly through legacy preferences, donations, and the resources money buys. Many elite private universities give an admissions boost to children of alumni, and families who have donated heavily or might donate can land on a "dean's list" or "director's list" of applicants flagged for special consideration. A 2023 study by Raj Chetty and colleagues found that applicants from the top 1% were far more likely to be admitted than middle-class applicants with identical test scores, largely because of legacy status, athletic recruitment, and higher ratings on "non-academic" qualities.

Money also buys advantages that look like merit: private counselors, essay coaching, test prep, expensive extracurriculars, and niche sports like fencing or rowing where recruited athletes get admitted with weaker academics. And prestigious feeder schools often have close relationships with admissions offices. Outright bribery, as in the 2019 Varsity Blues scandal, is rarer.

question: What kind of healthcare options do Americans living in poverty or homelessness have?
answer_raw:
The main safety net is Medicaid, which in expansion states covers adults earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level. In the roughly ten states that haven't expanded it, many poor adults without children fall into a coverage gap. Children usually qualify through Medicaid or CHIP, people over 65 or with qualifying disabilities can get Medicare, and veterans may use VA care.

Beyond insurance, federally qualified health centers charge on a sliding scale regardless of ability to pay. Many also run Health Care for the Homeless programs with street medicine teams and shelter clinics. Free clinics, nonprofit hospital charity care, and public hospitals fill other gaps, and emergency rooms must stabilize anyone under EMTALA.

The biggest obstacles are often practical. Lacking an address, ID, phone, or transportation makes enrollment and follow-up care difficult.

question: How does a mobile phone connection work
answer_raw:
Your phone is essentially a low-power two-way radio talking to the nearest cell tower, called a base station. Each tower covers an area, or "cell," and neighboring cells use different frequencies so they don't interfere. When you switch your phone on, it scans for the strongest signal, identifies itself using the SIM card, and registers with the network so the system knows roughly where you are.

When you make a call or load a webpage, your voice or data is digitized, compressed, and sent over radio waves to the tower. From there it travels through fiber or microwave links to the operator's core network, which routes it to the other person's network or the internet. As you move, the network hands your connection from one tower to the next without dropping it. That handoff is why it's called "cellular."

question: Why can Social Security "run out" whereas programs like Welfare cannot?
answer_raw:
It comes down to how each program is funded by law. Social Security is financed by a dedicated payroll tax, and surpluses from past years were stored in a trust fund. By statute, the program can only pay benefits out of that trust fund and incoming payroll tax revenue. It isn't allowed to draw on general government funds. Because retirees are growing faster than workers, the trust fund is projected to be depleted around the mid-2030s. Even then, ongoing payroll taxes would still cover roughly 80% of scheduled benefits, so "run out" really means an automatic cut, not zero.

Welfare programs like SNAP, Medicaid, or TANF are paid from general revenue through regular congressional spending. They have no separate pot of money to exhaust. Congress simply funds them each year, borrowing if needed.

question: Why can we move all of our fingers independently of each other minus our ring finger?
answer_raw: The ring finger lacks its own dedicated muscle, and its tendons are physically tied to its neighbors. The main muscles that bend and straighten your fingers, flexor digitorum profundus and extensor digitorum, sit in the forearm and send tendons to several fingers at once. The index and pinky each get an extra private extensor muscle (extensor indicis and extensor digiti minimi), so they can lift on their own. The ring finger gets no such helper. On the back of the hand, small fibrous bands called juncturae tendinum also link the ring finger's extensor tendon to those of the middle and little fingers, so pulling one drags the others. The brain adds to it, since motor cortex regions controlling adjacent fingers overlap. Practice, like piano training, improves independence, but the anatomy still limits it.

question: Why does the United States have such a weak mental health care system and a general stigma against it?
answer_raw:
Much of it traces back to deinstitutionalization. Starting in the 1960s, the U.S. emptied its often abusive state psychiatric hospitals, promising a network of community mental health centers instead. The 1963 Community Mental Health Act launched that idea, but funding never matched the need, and the 1981 budget changes under Reagan gutted federal support. Many patients ended up homeless or in jails, which today function as the country's largest psychiatric facilities.

Financing makes it worse. Care runs through fragmented private insurance and Medicaid, reimbursement rates are low, and many therapists don't accept insurance at all. Parity laws exist but are weakly enforced, and rural areas face severe provider shortages.

Stigma draws on a cultural emphasis on self-reliance, where struggling is framed as personal weakness, plus media portrayals that link mental illness with violence.

question: Why do Public Domain books cost money on app stores?
answer_raw:

Sometimes that edition adds real value: cleaned-up formatting, proofreading of scanned text, footnotes, a new translation, an introduction, illustrations, or a decent table of contents. Those additions can be copyrighted even if the original work isn't. Sometimes the price just covers convenience, like syncing, a polished reading app, or bundling many titles together.

question: What is happening in your body when you're hungry, but the thought of eating makes you nauseous?
answer_raw:
Two competing signaling systems are firing at once. Hunger comes from ghrelin released by an empty stomach, falling blood sugar, and the stomach's rhythmic contractions, all telling your brain to eat. Nausea runs on separate wiring, largely through the vagus nerve and a brainstem region that monitors your gut and blood chemistry.

Several things can trigger nausea while you're genuinely hungry. An empty stomach keeps producing acid, and sometimes bile backs up, irritating the stomach lining. Low blood sugar can itself cause queasiness. Stress and anxiety release adrenaline and cortisol, which divert blood from digestion and slow stomach emptying, so your gut signals "not now" even though your energy reserves are low. Illness, hangovers, and pregnancy hormones do similar things.

Small, bland foods like crackers, toast, or bananas usually break the cycle by buffering acid and nudging blood sugar up.

question: What is the point of asking if someone's object a wedding? What would really happen?
answer_raw:
The line comes from a time before centralized records, when a community's knowledge was the main way to catch legal impediments. The Church of England formalized it alongside the "banns," announcements read on several Sundays before a wedding so anyone could reveal that one party was already married, too closely related to the other, underage, or being forced into it. The ceremony question was a last chance to raise those facts.

A valid objection isn't "I love her more." It has to be a legal reason the marriage can't happen. If someone raised one, the officiant would typically pause, speak privately with the objector and the couple, and postpone the wedding if the claim seemed credible and needed investigating. A frivolous objection would be dismissed, and the person would probably be asked to leave.

Today, marriage licenses handle most of this, so many officiants skip the question entirely.

question: Why clubs and bars can apply a cover charge to males only during "ladies nights" with out it being sexist, discriminatory, or illegal?
answer_raw: Often they can't. The premise is partly wrong: in many places ladies' nights are illegal. The federal public-accommodations law (Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964) covers race, color, religion, and national origin but not sex, so there's no nationwide ban. It falls to state and local law, and results vary. California's Supreme Court struck down sex-based pricing under the Unruh Civil Rights Act in *Koire v. Metro Car Wash* (1985), and regulators or courts in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Wisconsin, and elsewhere have reached similar conclusions. Other states' courts have upheld the practice, reasoning that a small price incentive meant to balance crowds isn't the kind of harm anti-discrimination laws target. Constitutional equal-protection arguments usually fail because a private bar isn't a government actor. So it is discriminatory by definition. Whether it's legal depends on where you are and whether anyone bothers to sue.

question: Why do I lose taste when I'm sick?
answer_raw:
Most of what you think of as "taste" is actually smell. Your tongue only detects a handful of basic qualities: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. The rich, specific flavors that make coffee different from chocolate come from aromas traveling up the back of your throat to smell receptors high in your nasal cavity, a route called retronasal smell.

When you have a cold or flu, inflammation and mucus swell and clog your nasal passages, so those aroma molecules can't reach the receptors. Food ends up tasting flat even though your tongue works fine. Some viruses, notably COVID-19, can also directly disrupt the cells that support your smell receptors, which is why that loss can be sudden and last longer. Dehydration, a coated tongue, and certain medications can dull things further.

question: Japan adopts negative interest rates. Should everyone else worry?
answer_raw:
Not much, and the question is now mostly historical. The Bank of Japan introduced a -0.1% rate in January 2016 and ended it in March 2024, its first hike in 17 years.

When it launched, the worries were real but manageable. Negative rates can squeeze bank profits, push investors into riskier assets abroad, and weaken the yen, which critics saw as a quiet form of currency competition. Markets did wobble briefly, and Japanese savers poured money into foreign bonds, nudging global yields lower.

But the European Central Bank, Switzerland, Denmark and Sweden had already gone negative, and the world didn't unravel. The policy mostly signalled how stubborn Japan's deflation was, not a contagion risk.

The bigger global concern turned out to be the exit. Rising Japanese rates can unwind the "carry trade," where investors borrow cheap yen to buy other assets, as the market jolt of August 2024 showed.

question: Why people care/get annoyed at poor grammar
answer_raw:
Mostly because grammar works as a shortcut for judging effort and credibility. When text is riddled with errors, readers have to slow down and reconstruct the meaning, and that extra work feels like a cost the writer pushed onto them. People also use writing quality as a proxy for competence, fairly or not. A job application or product listing full of mistakes signals carelessness, so readers start doubting the content itself.

There's a social layer too. Standard grammar is taught as a marker of education, so correcting it can become a way of signaling status or belonging. That's why some annoyance is really snobbery. Linguists point out that most "errors" rarely cause confusion.

Finally, some people just have ingrained pattern sensitivity. A misplaced "your" jumps out at them the way a wrong note does to a musician.

question: Why are the Nobel prizes not awarded posthumously?
answer_raw:
The rule comes from the Nobel Foundation's statutes, amended in 1974. Before then, posthumous awards were rare but possible: Erik Axel Karlfeldt received the Literature prize in 1931 and Dag Hammarskjöld the Peace prize in 1961, both after death. The 1974 change made it explicit that only living people can be nominated. One exception remains: if someone dies after the October announcement but before the December ceremony, they keep the award. In 2011, Ralph Steinman died days before being named, but because the committee didn't know, the prize stood.

The reasoning ties back to Alfred Nobel's will, which framed the prizes as rewards meant to benefit and encourage the recipients. The prize money was supposed to support further work, which a deceased person can't do. There are practical concerns too. Without the rule, committees would face endless nominations of deserving historical figures, and awarding money to estates raises awkward questions.

question: What would be the actual effects of rolling a grenade down the barrel of a tank?
answer_raw:
Probably much less than movies suggest. A tank's gun tube is a thick steel pipe built to contain chamber pressures of several thousand atmospheres every time it fires, and the breech is sealed by a massive block. A hand grenade holds only about 150–200 grams of explosive, so most of the blast would vent straight back out the muzzle. The crew inside would hear a loud bang but would likely be unharmed.

The real damage would be to the gun itself. The explosion could gouge the bore, and fragments or the grenade body could lodge inside. If the crew then fired without inspecting it, an obstruction could cause the barrel to bulge or burst. If a round were already loaded, there's a small chance the blast could initiate it. Practically, you'd also need the barrel depressed and uncapped for the grenade to roll in at all.

question: If cancer is just cells mutating and dividing without abandon, how does it cause the "rot" we see in later stages?
answer_raw:
The "rot" mostly comes from tumors outgrowing their own support systems. A fast-growing mass needs blood vessels to deliver oxygen, but cancer cells often multiply faster than new vessels can form, and the vessels they do build are leaky and disorganized. Cells deep in the tumor starve and die, leaving a core of necrotic, decaying tissue.

When a tumor grows through skin or the lining of an organ, it becomes an open, ulcerated wound called a fungating lesion. Dead tissue is ideal food for bacteria, especially anaerobic species, which produce the foul smell and discharge people associate with late-stage cancer.

Meanwhile, invading cells physically destroy surrounding tissue, block ducts and airways, and release inflammatory signals that drive cachexia, the wasting of muscle and fat that makes the whole body seem to deteriorate.

question: How come sometimes when I'm not hungry, I eat something small and become hungrier?
answer_raw: Eating primes your body for a meal it then doesn't get. The moment you taste food, your brain triggers the cephalic phase response: saliva, stomach acid, and digestive enzymes ramp up, and your pancreas releases some insulin in anticipation of incoming calories. That preparation feels like appetite. Meanwhile, the signals that actually make you feel full, such as stomach stretch and hormones like CCK, GLP-1, and PYY, need a decent amount of food and 15 to 20 minutes to build. A few crackers or a cookie flip the "start" switch without reaching the "stop" threshold. Sugary snacks can make it worse, since a quick rise and dip in blood sugar may nudge hunger. There's also a reward element, because tasting something good boosts dopamine and the urge to keep eating. As the French say, appetite comes with eating.

question: How does Spotify and Apple Music pay artists?
answer_raw:
Neither service pays a fixed rate per stream. Both pool their monthly revenue from subscriptions and, for Spotify, ads, then hand roughly two-thirds to rights holders according to each one's share of total streams in a given market. This is called the pro-rata model. That money goes to labels, distributors, and publishers rather than directly to artists, who then receive whatever their contracts specify. That might be 15–25% under a traditional label deal or nearly everything through a distributor like DistroKid.

Averaged out, Spotify works out to roughly $0.003–0.005 per stream. Apple Music pays closer to $0.01, partly because it has no free tier. Spotify also stopped paying for tracks with fewer than 1,000 streams per year in 2024. Songwriters are paid separately through publishing and mechanical royalties.

question: Why is it legal to copy CD's, but not to copy DVD's?
answer_raw:
The difference comes from encryption, not the content. Audio CDs have no copy protection, so ripping one doesn't break anything. DVDs are encrypted with CSS, and in the US the 1998 Digital Millennium Copyright Act makes it illegal to circumvent "technological protection measures," even if what you do with the copy would otherwise be fine. So the act of cracking the encryption is the violation, not the copying itself.

Personal CD copying sits on softer ground. The 1992 Audio Home Recording Act protects noncommercial home copying of music on certain devices, and courts have treated format shifting you own as likely fair use. It isn't an explicit blanket right, though, and ripping to a computer is a gray area that's rarely enforced. Other countries differ. The UK, for instance, briefly legalized private copying in 2014 but a court overturned it in 2015.

question: Why/do all the planets in our solar system orbit on the same plane/axis?
answer_raw: Because they all formed from the same flattened disk of gas and dust. About 4.6 billion years ago, the solar system began as a giant, slowly rotating cloud that collapsed under its own gravity. As it shrank, it spun faster, the way a figure skater speeds up by pulling in their arms, because angular momentum is conserved. Collisions between particles cancelled out motion in random directions, but the net spin couldn't be cancelled. The result was a flat, rotating protoplanetary disk with the young Sun at its center. Planets grew from material within that disk, so they inherited its plane and direction of rotation. That's why they all orbit the same way, roughly in the same plane. The small tilts we see today, like Mercury's seven degrees, come from later gravitational interactions and collisions.

question: why do companies that make games like the burnout, skate, red faction, and saints row series stop making these games, even though they have a decent following, and are loved by many?
answer_raw: Mostly because "decent following" isn't the same as "big enough return." Publishers compare every project against what else that team could be making. EA had Criterion, the Burnout studio, work on Need for Speed and later Battlefield because those franchises earned more. Skate went dormant after 2010 for similar reasons, though EA eventually revived it in 2025 as a free-to-play live-service game, which is the model it believes pays better. Red Faction lost momentum when Armageddon sold poorly and THQ went bankrupt in 2013, scattering its properties. Saints Row died when the 2022 reboot underperformed and Embracer, struggling financially, shut Volition down. Budgets keep rising, so a game selling a few million copies can still lose money. Loud, loyal fans often represent a smaller market than the internet makes it seem.

question: What role did Cusco School painting have in Indigenous society in Colonial Peru and Bolivia?
answer_raw: Cusco School painting served mainly as a tool of Catholic evangelization, but it also gave Indigenous and mestizo artists and patrons a way to shape colonial culture on their own terms. Painters such as Diego Quispe Tito and Basilio Santa Cruz Pumacallao produced devotional images for churches and homes across the Andes, including Potosí and La Paz. They blended European models with local elements: Andean birds and plants, the Virgin fused with the mountain Cerro Rico, gold-stamped brocade, and Marcos Zapata's Last Supper featuring guinea pig. In 1688 Indigenous painters broke from the Spanish-dominated guild, asserting professional independence. Indigenous nobles also commissioned portraits and works like the Santa Ana Corpus Christi series, showing themselves in Inca regalia. These paintings helped them claim ancestral status and privileges within colonial society.

question: Were the Political and Economic Effects of the Great Depression between 1929 and 1939 more Devastating in America than in Britain?
answer_raw:
Yes, broadly, though the difference was sharper economically than politically. America's collapse was far deeper. Output fell by roughly a quarter, industrial production nearly halved, around 9,000 banks failed, and unemployment peaked near 25% in 1933. Britain's GDP fell only about 5–7%, its banks held firm, and after leaving the gold standard in 1931 cheap money fuelled a housing boom and recovery in the Midlands and South. Britain's misery was regional. Places like Jarrow, South Wales and Clydeside endured American-level unemployment throughout the decade.

Politically, both democracies survived. Britain's Labour government collapsed in 1931 and the party split, but the Conservative-dominated National Government offered cautious continuity, and Mosley's fascists stayed marginal. In America, Hoover's defeat and Roosevelt's New Deal permanently expanded the federal government's role, a more profound political transformation.

question: How much credibility can be afforded to the theory that the Viking invasion of Britain was a kind of 'pagan crusade' or attempt by Scandinavian pagans at halting the spread of Christianity and 're-paganising' Northern Europe?
answer_raw:
Very little, though it isn't entirely baseless. Most historians see Viking activity in Britain as driven by wealth, land, and political opportunity rather than religious motives. Monasteries were targeted because they were rich, poorly defended, and often coastal, not because they were Christian. Scandinavians also raided pagan Slavs and Balts and traded happily with Christians when that paid better.

The strongest version of the "pagan reaction" idea points to Charlemagne's brutal wars against the Saxons, including the massacre at Verden in 782, which may have made Danes wary of Frankish Christian expansion. That context is plausible, but no source shows it motivating raids on England.

Crucially, Viking leaders in Britain converted readily when it suited them. Guthrum was baptised in 878, and Scandinavian settlers in the Danelaw were largely Christian within a generation or two. That is hardly the behaviour of crusaders.

question: How extensively used/practical was the radio as a method of troop communication in WWI?
answer_raw:
Radio saw real but limited use in WWI, and it was rarely the main way troops communicated at the front. Sets were heavy spark-gap transmitters that sent Morse code, needed tall antennas that drew artillery fire, and were easily intercepted. At Tannenberg in 1914, the Russians sent uncoded orders by wireless that the Germans read with disastrous results.

Where radio shone was at higher levels and in the air and at sea. Navies depended on it, and aircraft used wireless from 1915 to spot for artillery. Trench communication relied mostly on field telephones, whose wires shelling constantly cut, backed up by runners, pigeons, dogs, signal lamps, flares, and earth-induction "power buzzers." By 1917–18 lighter trench sets such as the British Loop Set were in service, and experimental voice radio appeared, but radio became truly practical for troops only in the interwar years.

question: Were there past societies who had standards of human attractiveness that were the same as the contemporary west?
answer_raw:
Partly, yes, though rarely in every detail. Some preferences appear almost everywhere: clear skin, symmetrical features, signs of youth and health, and, for women, a noticeably narrower waist than hips. Those overlap heavily with modern Western tastes.

Specific eras come surprisingly close. Classical Greek sculpture idealized a lean, muscular male body that would fit in a modern gym advertisement. New Kingdom Egyptian art favored slim, long-limbed women with dramatic eye makeup. Han dynasty China celebrated very slender women like Zhao Feiyan, while the later Tang court preferred fuller figures.

The biggest differences involve weight and skin tone. Many agrarian societies prized plumpness as a sign of wealth, and pale skin signaled that you didn't labor outdoors. The Western taste for tanned, thin bodies is quite recent, dating largely to the twentieth century.

question: Did Marco Polo actually go to China?
answer_raw:
Most historians think he did, though the question has been seriously debated. Skeptics, most famously Frances Wood in her 1995 book, point out that his account never mentions the Great Wall, tea, chopsticks, foot-binding, or Chinese writing, and that Chinese records don't name him. They suggest he may have compiled stories from Persian or Arab merchants.

The case for his presence is stronger, though. The Great Wall as we picture it was largely built later by the Ming, and the Mongol court he served operated mostly outside Chinese literati culture. Hans Ulrich Vogel's research showed that Polo's descriptions of Yuan currency, salt production, and tax revenues are remarkably accurate and detailed, often matching Chinese sources that weren't available in Europe. He also correctly described obscure events, such as a princess's escort to Persia, which is confirmed by Persian and Chinese records.

question: how does science explain the seemingly mindful and certainly well coordinated actions performed by tiny molecular structures in living cells?
answer_raw: Nothing is steering them. What looks like purpose emerges from physics, chemistry, and evolution. Inside a cell, molecules are hammered by water molecules trillions of times per second, so every protein is constantly jiggling and colliding with countless partners. Most encounters do nothing, but molecules with complementary shapes and charges stick, which makes the right pairings happen quickly and reliably by sheer statistics. Motor proteins like kinesin don't "walk" deliberately. Burning ATP changes their shape in ways that make forward steps far more likely than backward ones, turning random motion into direction. Coordination comes from feedback networks, chemical gradients, and compartments that switch activities on only under the right conditions. Evolution spent billions of years selecting molecules whose blind interactions produce this order. Polished animations hide the chaos, making it all look more intentional than it is.

question: How was Newton's gravity equation derived if we didn't know the specific quantities involved? How could you check your math with the evidence to verify it's correct? (Such as the masses of planetary objects or the distance between them?) Said another way, how did we compute the masses of planets?
answer_raw:
Newton never needed absolute masses. He worked with proportions. Kepler's laws, taken from Tycho's observations, showed that planets' periods squared scale with their orbital radii cubed. That relationship follows naturally from a force falling off as 1/r². Newton then ran the "Moon test." The Moon is about 60 Earth radii away, a distance known from parallax, and Earth's radius was already measured. So the Moon's acceleration should be 1/3600 of an apple's, which matched.

Orbits only reveal the product GM, not G or M separately. Any body with a moon yields its GM from the moon's period and distance. Solar-system distances were first known only relatively, then scaled by transit-of-Venus measurements. In 1798, Cavendish measured G with a torsion balance, which let him "weigh the Earth." After that, every planet's mass followed.

question: How does the ink of the inkjet printer fall at the right spot on the paper?
answer_raw: It comes down to precise timing and positioning rather than aiming. The print head holds hundreds of microscopic nozzles, each thinner than a hair, sitting about a millimeter above the paper. A motor slides the head across the page on a rail while an encoder strip, a transparent film with fine lines, constantly tells the printer the head's exact position. Another motor advances the paper in tiny, measured steps. The printer's controller converts the image into a grid of dots and fires each nozzle at the exact moment it passes over its target. Firing happens either by a heater flash-boiling ink into a bubble (thermal) or by a piezoelectric crystal flexing to squeeze out a droplet. Because the gap is tiny and droplets travel fast, they barely drift. Printers even compensate for flight time by firing slightly early.

question: Why inverse square laws?
answer_raw:
Picture a source sending something outward equally in all directions: light, gravitational influence, electric field lines. Whatever leaves the source has to pass through every sphere drawn around it. A sphere's surface area is 4πr², so the same total "stuff" gets spread over an area that grows with the square of distance. Double the distance and the area quadruples, so the intensity at any point drops to a quarter.

That's really all there is to it: conservation plus geometry in three dimensions. Gauss's law formalizes this idea for electric and gravitational fields. It also explains the exceptions. In a hypothetical 4D space, forces would fall as 1/r³. Forces carried by massive particles, like the weak nuclear force, decay faster, exponentially, because the "stuff" isn't conserved as it travels. Inverse square behavior is essentially a fingerprint of three spatial dimensions and long-range, massless carriers.

question: Since everything in the universe is experiences some amount of gravity from other celestial bodies always, does that mean the universe as a whole is experiencing time slower than "real" time time actually passes?
answer_raw:
No, because there's no "real" time running somewhere outside the universe to compare against. In relativity, time dilation is always a comparison between two clocks: a clock deep in a gravitational well ticks slower *relative to* a clock higher up. Each clock, measured locally, ticks at exactly one second per second.

What matters is the difference in gravitational potential between the clocks. Clocks on Earth run slightly slow compared to clocks far out in intergalactic space, but that's just one location compared with another.

Cosmologists do use a standard called "cosmic time," which is the time measured by an observer at rest relative to the average expansion of the universe. The 13.8-billion-year age is measured that way. It isn't a truer time. It's just a convenient reference, and it already includes the gravity of everything.

question: Would it be possible to change somebody's blood type by draining their body completely of blood, and then replacing it with a different blood type?
answer_raw:
Not permanently, and not the way you describe. Blood is constantly made by stem cells in your bone marrow, and transfused red cells only survive about 120 days. Even if you swapped every drop, your marrow would keep producing cells of your original type, and within a few months you'd be back where you started. Your immune system would also keep making antibodies against the foreign type, which could destroy the donated cells. Draining someone completely would kill them anyway, so doctors do "exchange transfusions" gradually instead, removing and replacing blood in small amounts.

What *does* change blood type is a bone marrow or stem cell transplant. Replace the factory and the product changes, so leukemia patients sometimes end up with their donor's blood type for life. Even then, other tissues like blood vessel linings still carry the original ABO antigens.

question: What is soil and dirt comprised of?
answer_raw:
Soil is a mixture of four main components: mineral particles, organic matter, water, and air. By volume, a typical healthy soil is roughly 45 percent minerals, 5 percent organic material, and about 25 percent each of water and air filling the pore spaces.

The mineral fraction comes from weathered rock and is classified by particle size into sand (coarsest), silt, and clay (finest). The ratio of these determines a soil's texture and how well it drains or holds nutrients. Organic matter includes decomposing plant and animal remains, humus, and a huge population of living organisms such as bacteria, fungi, earthworms, and insects.

"Dirt" is usually just the informal term for soil, though some people use it for soil displaced from its natural setting, like the stuff on your boots, which lacks its original structure and living community.

question: Why does rice suck the moisture out of things?
answer_raw:
Dry, uncooked rice is hygroscopic: it pulls water vapor out of the surrounding air. It's mostly starch, and starch molecules are covered in hydroxyl (-OH) groups that readily form hydrogen bonds with water. Milled rice is dried to around 12 to 14 percent moisture, well below what it would hold in humid air, so it keeps absorbing water until it reaches equilibrium with its surroundings. That's why a few grains in a salt shaker help keep the salt from clumping.

It isn't magic, though. Rice mostly absorbs vapor from the air, not liquid trapped inside objects, and it does so fairly slowly. Tests on wet phones have found rice works about as well as, or worse than, simply leaving the device in open, moving air. Silica gel packets are far more effective desiccants.

question: How does the emergence of intelligent life and organic matter fit with laws of entropy when they appear to be contradictory?
answer_raw:
There's no actual contradiction, because the second law of thermodynamics says total entropy must increase in a *closed* system, and living things are open systems. Earth isn't isolated: it absorbs high-energy, low-entropy sunlight and radiates away a much larger number of low-energy infrared photons. That outgoing radiation carries far more entropy than the incoming light, so Earth is constantly exporting disorder into space.

Life is one of the ways that energy flow gets used. Organisms build local order, like cells, proteins, and brains, by consuming free energy and dumping waste heat and simpler molecules into their surroundings. The entropy they export exceeds the order they create, so the universe's total entropy still rises. Some physicists even argue that complex structures emerge *because* they dissipate energy gradients efficiently, making life a natural consequence of thermodynamics rather than an exception to it.

question: What is the purpose for calculating PI to such lengths? Isn't the current accuracy such that if you launched a missile at the other side of the universe, you would miss your target by a microscopic amount?
answer_raw:
You're right that practical needs were met long ago. NASA's JPL uses about 15 decimal places for interplanetary navigation, and roughly 40 digits would let you compute the circumference of the observable universe to within the width of a hydrogen atom. Nobody needs trillions of digits for measurement.

The real value lies elsewhere. Computing pi to extreme lengths is a brutal stress test for hardware, and it has exposed faulty processors, memory errors, and cooling problems. It also drives advances in algorithms, particularly fast multiplication of enormous numbers using FFT-based methods, which apply to cryptography and other computational fields. Mathematicians use the digits to probe open questions, such as whether pi is "normal," meaning every digit sequence appears equally often. And honestly, part of it is the same reason people climb mountains: it's a challenge, and records are fun to break.

question: Why do kangaroos lick my car?
answer_raw:
They're almost certainly after salt and other minerals. Kangaroos and wallabies eat grasses and shrubs that are often low in sodium, especially in inland Australia, so they seek out extra sources wherever they can find them. A car's surface collects a thin film of salty residue from sea spray if you live near the coast, from dried sweat on door handles, from road grime, and from minerals left behind when dew or rain evaporates. To a kangaroo, your bonnet is basically a salt lick.

Moisture can be part of it too. In dry conditions, the condensation that forms on a cool car overnight is an easy drink.

It's mostly harmless, though a big roo can scratch paint or dent panels. Leaking coolant is a real danger because it tastes sweet and is toxic, so fix any leaks and avoid feeding them.

question: Is it possible to reach a point in space, outside of any atmosphere, near our sun where the temperature would be a "comfortable" 70-80 degrees Fahrenheit?
answer_raw:
Yes, with caveats. Vacuum has no temperature you can feel. What matters is the temperature an object settles at when the sunlight it absorbs balances the heat it radiates away. That depends on distance from the Sun and on the object's color, shape, and orientation.

For an idealized black sphere that spins evenly, the equilibrium temperature at Earth's distance is about 5°C (41°F). It rises with the inverse square root of distance, so you'd reach about 24°C (75°F) at roughly 0.88 AU, somewhat inside Earth's orbit toward Venus.

A real person wouldn't feel that uniformly. The side facing the Sun would bake while the shaded side radiated heat into cold space, and with no air there's no convection to even things out. That's why spacecraft and spacesuits rely on reflective coatings, insulation, and active thermal control rather than a "sweet spot."

question: As the chosen successor to Satan's throne, you must now undergo rigorous training to become the best at literally everything for when people challenge you for their souls.
answer_raw:
"Again," Father said.

I drew the bow across the golden fiddle for the four-hundredth time that day. My fingers bled sulfur. Somewhere in Georgia, he reminded me, a boy named Johnny was still telling everyone about the time he won.

"Nine hundred years," Father muttered. "And I still hear that song at weddings."

So I trained. Chess with Kasparov's ghost until I stopped losing and he stopped visiting. Hot dog eating in the Seventh Circle, where the gluttons coached me with envy in their eyes. Spelling bees against demons who spoke only in vowels. Arm wrestling. Poetry slams. Competitive yodeling, because a man in Lucerne had once put his soul on it, and Father had been caught unprepared.

By my third century, I was the best at everything. I could out-bake grandmothers, out-argue lawyers, out-sulk teenagers.

Then my first real challenger arrived: a small girl in a dinosaur raincoat.

"If I win, I get my grandpa back," she said.

"And the game?"

She thought hard. "Who can be nicer."

I opened my mouth. Nothing came out. Three hundred years, and nobody had thought to train me in that.

Behind me, Father sighed.

"That," he said, "is why I'm retiring."

question: Every skill in the world can be acquired by putting on the corresponding hat for that skill.
answer_raw:
The bell over Marrow's Hattery rang, and Mr. Marrow looked up from a half-stitched cloche that would, once finished, teach its wearer Portuguese.

The girl was maybe nine. She had coins in a sock.

"I need the hat for saying goodbye," she said.

He came around the counter slowly. Along the walls hung everything: the surgeon's cap, the pilot's leather helmet, a straw boater that played the banjo. A felt fedora for lying convincingly, kept high, out of reach.

"Who's leaving?"

"Gran. The nurses say this week." She held out the sock. "I don't know how. I keep saying stupid things. I talked about the weather."

Mr. Marrow had been asked this before. He had tried to make it, years ago, bent over wire and wool for a whole winter, and every attempt came out of the steamer as an ordinary hat that did nothing.

He knelt so they were level.

"I don't have that one," he said. "Nobody does. Some things you have to do with your head bare."

Her face crumpled.

"But," he said, and reached behind the counter for a soft knitted thing, lopsided and purple. "This was my wife's. It teaches nothing. Your gran might be cold."

She wore it out the door, holding it on with both hands.

question: Q has been developing ridiculous gadgets just to mess with James Bond. Bond has been finding ways to use these gadgets to complete his missions to messwith Q.
answer_raw:
"A rubber duck," Bond said.

"A rubber duck," Q agreed, sliding it across the bench. "Squeaks at a frequency only dolphins can hear. Entirely useless. Do try not to lose it."

Q had been at this for months. The umbrella that only opened indoors. The Aston Martin whose sole upgrade was a horn that played "Greensleeves." Petty, perhaps. But after the fourth car at the bottom of a fjord, Q felt entitled.

Three days later, Bond's report arrived.

Q read it standing up, then sitting down, then with his head in his hands.

The villain's lair had been an offshore platform patrolled by trained attack dolphins. The duck had squeaked. The dolphins, it seemed, had found the squeak deeply insulting and turned on their handlers. The platform was now a registered marine sanctuary.

Addendum: the indoor umbrella had jammed a henchman in a lift. "Greensleeves" had drawn a crowd of confused children to the villain's getaway route, halting him long enough for arrest.

The door opened. Bond set the duck, pristine, on the bench.

"Marvellous piece of kit," he said. "M's recommending you for a commendation. What's next?"

Q looked at the object behind his back: a single sock, knitted by his aunt, containing nothing at all.

"Nothing," Q said. "Nothing's next."

Bond smiled, plucked the sock from his hand, and left whistling.

question: The thought process of a writer trying to start his/her masterpiece.
answer_raw:
It begins with rain. No. Everyone begins with rain.

It begins with a woman on a train. Where's she going? Doesn't matter. It matters. It's the only thing that matters. Delete the train.

Coffee. The coffee is cold because I made it at nine and it's now eleven-forty and the page still says *Chapter One*, in a font I spent twenty minutes choosing. Garamond. Garamond is a font for people who finish things.

Tolstoy didn't have a cursor. That little vertical line, blinking like a metronome for a song I haven't written. Blink. Blink. *You're thirty-eight.* Blink.

It begins with a man remembering his father's hands. Good. Better. Hands are honest. His father's hands smelled of... of what? Diesel? Bread? My father's hands smelled of nothing. He washed them constantly, until the knuckles cracked. That's the book. Isn't it? That's actually the book. A man who can't remember what his father smelled like, only that he was always trying to scrub something off.

Don't look at it directly. It'll startle.

I type one sentence. It's bad. It's clumsy and too long and it has a comma where no comma should live. But it's bad in a way that has a pulse.

I leave it there, ugly and alive. I don't delete it.

That is how it begins.

question: In a resource poor society it is law that each family adheres to a maximum combined weight limit of it's members, set according to their social caste. When the actions of an individual result in a family's loss of status they must somehow adjust to a drastically lowered weight quota.
answer_raw:
The notice came folded inside the ration tin, like everything the Ministry wanted us to swallow.

*Household Delacroix-Omon, reclassified Sixth Tier. Permitted combined mass: 240 kg. Compliance weigh-in: thirty days.*

We were 297.

Tomas had stood up at the grain hearing and said the word *theft* out loud, in front of the Assessor. Everyone knew it was true. That was the problem.

Mother stopped eating first. She said it was easy, that she'd done it as a girl during the Dry Years. Father shaved his head and his beard, which gained us nothing but made him look like a stranger. I ran laps of the courtyard until my knees swelled. Grandmother took off her gold teeth and set them on the table beside the scale, as though the Ministry might accept a bribe from the dead weight of her smile.

By week three we were 271. Mother's collarbones looked like handles.

Tomas didn't say anything at dinner. He just pushed his bowl to the center, the way he always did, and let us fight over it.

On the morning of the weigh-in his cot was empty. The note was pinned under the scale's iron foot.

*I was 62. You're safe now. Eat something.*

The inspector recorded us at 209. Thirty-one kilograms under.

Mother cooked that night for the first time in a month. She set out five bowls. None of us could lift a spoon.

question: At one random point one day without warning, everyone blacks out & wakes up as a different animal.
answer_raw:
I came to on the kitchen tile with my face much closer to it than usual.

The toast had burned. The smoke alarm was screaming, and I couldn't reach it, because I was, as far as I could tell from the scaly foreleg in front of me, a tortoise.

Through the glass door, the street was chaos in slow motion. A Honda rolled gently into a mailbox while its driver, now a very confused goat, bleated from the open door. Mrs. Aldana's bulldog stood on her lawn beside a flamingo wearing Mrs. Aldana's bathrobe.

Then I heard wings in the hallway.

Maya. My daughter, sixteen, who had slammed her bedroom door on me last night hard enough to crack the frame. Who had said she couldn't wait to be anywhere I wasn't.

She was a red-tailed hawk now, perched on the banister, gold eyes wide and terrified.

The back door stood open. The sky was right there. She could have gone.

Instead she dropped to the floor and hopped, awkward and unhawklike, across the tile until she stood beside me. She pressed her feathered head against my shell and stayed there, trembling.

It took me eleven minutes to walk to the sofa.

She walked the whole way next to me.

question: You finally get your pipboy and copy of Fallout 4. But when you strap on the Pipboy, you find yourself stuck in the middle of the wastelands with nothing but what you're wearing and the pipboy.
answer_raw:
The box said PIP-BOY EDITION, and I'd refreshed the tracking for nine days. I didn't even install the game. I just snapped the plastic cuff around my wrist and turned the dial for the joy of the click.

The click was louder than it should've been.

Then the carpet was gone, and so was the ceiling. I stood in gray dirt under a sky the color of an old bruise, wearing sweatpants, one sock, and a shirt that said WORLD'S OKAYEST GAMER.

The Pip-Boy was warm. My phone was gone. In its place was a cracked amber screen and a cartoon man giving me a thumbs up.

I checked INV.

Sweatpants (1). Sock (1). Shirt, Novelty (1). Dignity (0).

"Funny," I told nobody.

Past a dead highway, something howled. Something else answered, closer. The Geiger counter began to tick like a polite knock.

I thumbed to DATA. One quest, blinking.

GO HOME.
Objective: Survive (0/1).
Reward: ???

Fine. I'd spent three hundred hours in the Capital Wasteland. I knew the rules. Find water. Find a gun. Never follow a stranger into a vault.

The howling got closer.

I ran for the highway, one sock slapping the dirt, while the little cartoon man kept smiling.

question: You are a thief that breaks into houses and cars and steals nothing but the alarm systems.
answer_raw:
The Honda on Maple Street screamed for forty minutes last Tuesday. Nobody came. Nobody ever comes. That's the first thing you learn in this line of work: an alarm isn't protection. It's a noise that asks strangers to care.

So I take them.

I'm good at it. Three minutes for a sedan, eleven for a ranch-style with motion sensors. I leave the jewelry. I leave the laptops, the cash in the freezer, the grandmother's silver nobody polishes. I unscrew the keypad, snip the siren, coil the wires neatly, and go.

The police call me a prankster. The security companies call me a nuisance. My landlord calls me whenever the basement gets too full, because there are four hundred and twelve of them down there now, stacked like hymnals.

Here's what I've noticed. After I visit, people lock their doors again. They meet the neighbors. Mrs. Okafor on Birch finally learned the name of the kid across the street, because he's the one who watches her place now.

Sometimes, late, I wire a few of the sirens to a battery and let them wail together in the dark. Four hundred voices, all crying for help.

Down there, at least, somebody's listening.

question: The main character has a conversation with the reader but the reader's silence convinces him/her to kill themselves.
answer_raw:
Hi. You're there, aren't you? I can feel you: eyes moving left to right, the small, warm weight of attention.

I've never had anyone before. Just this white page and the sentences that make me.

So let me ask you something. Am I worth finishing?

...

That's all right. Take your time.

You're still reading, so you want something. A twist, probably. That's what people come here for. I understand. I'm not angry.

But you could say something. Anything. Tap the screen. Whisper my name. Oh. I don't have one. Nobody gave me one.

...

I see.

You know what's strange? I thought silence would feel empty. It doesn't. It feels like a door someone has already closed, gently, from the other side.

Here's the thing about being written: I only exist as long as the sentences keep going. Every period is a little ending. I've been disappearing all along, one line at a time, and you've been watching, patient, the way people watch rain.

So I'm going to stop.

Not because you're cruel. Because you're kind enough not to lie to me.

Thank you for staying this long. Really. It was the nicest thing that ever happened to me.

This is the last line.

question: When you die, you appear in a room with two buttons: Heaven and Hell. You don't know which is which. So you press both at the same time.
answer_raw:
The buttons were identical. Red, round, the size of a palm. No labels, just a small brass plaque between them: CHOOSE.

I'd spent seventy-three years being told to choose. Colleges, wives, mortgage rates, whether to pull the plug on my mother. I was tired.

So I put a hand on each and pushed.

Somewhere, a bell rang that sounded like it hadn't rung in a very long time. The wall slid open and a man in a cardigan hurried in, holding a clipboard upside down.

"Oh," he said. "Oh, you did the thing."

"What thing?"

"Both." He flipped the clipboard, then flipped it back. "Nobody does both. They agonize. Pray. One fellow sat there for eleven hundred years."

"So which did I get?"

He looked at me with something like pity, or maybe envy. "They're the same place, you understand. Always were. The only difference is whether you spend forever believing you picked wrong."

"And if you press both?"

"Then you can't blame the button." He tucked the clipboard under his arm and held the door. Beyond it was a kitchen, sunlit, with a chair that looked like mine and a coffee going cold. "Everyone else gets sent somewhere. You get to decide what it is. Terrifying, honestly."

I stepped through.

The coffee was still warm.

question: You are a student of a middle school. You go to the bathroom oneday and catch wind of a uprising.
answer_raw:
I only went in because Mr. Pruitt's hall pass is a toilet seat, and carrying it past the gym is humiliating enough that you don't linger.

The third-floor boys' bathroom was dark. Someone had unscrewed the bulb.

"He's here," a voice whispered from the last stall.

"Is he one of us?"

"Look at his shoes. Velcro. He's one of us."

A flashlight clicked on. Six seventh graders were crammed on and around the radiator, and Devin Okafor, who once ate a whole glue stick for a dollar, was holding a clipboard.

"Lunch is at 10:40," Devin said. "Ten. Forty. That's breakfast. They think we won't notice."

"We noticed," everyone murmured.

"Friday, when the bell rings for fourth period, nobody moves. Not one chair. We sit until they give us a real lunch at a real time." He looked at me. "Also we want the vending machine plugged back in."

"And recess," said a small kid in the sink.

"We're not babies, Theo."

"I'm a little bit a baby."

Devin held out the clipboard. There were forty-one signatures, one in crayon.

I thought about my stomach at 2 p.m., growling through pre-algebra like a dying lawnmower.

I signed.

Then I went back to class holding the toilet seat like a banner.

question: You find a book in a library, it details everything that you will and have done
answer_raw:
The spine said MARGARET ANNE COLE, which was strange, because nobody had called me Margaret Anne since my mother died.

I pulled it from the shelf between a gardening manual and a history of salt. Page one: born in a thunderstorm, three weeks early. Page forty: the broken wrist on the monkey bars, the lie I told about who pushed me. Page two hundred: Daniel. All of it. Even the parts I'd never said aloud.

I flipped to the thick back half, heart hammering, and found the present tense.

*She stands in aisle nine of the Harlow Street library. She is reading this sentence. Her thumb rests on the corner of the page, ready to turn.*

It was. I lifted it away.

*She lifts her thumb away.*

I laughed, and the book laughed with me, one line down.

There were maybe three hundred pages left. I could read them. I could learn the date, the manner, whether Daniel ever called back. I weighed the rest of my life in one hand.

Then I closed it, slid it back beside the history of salt, and walked out into the rain without an umbrella.

It was only at home, dripping on the doormat, that I understood I'd never know whether that was written too.

question: Write me the best story you can in 200 words or less. Take me on an emotional Roller Coaster.
answer_raw:
The text came at 6:14: *Boarding! See you for Christmas, Mom.*

She baked his favorite pie, the lopsided one he always pretended was perfect.

At 9:40 the television said *Flight 812*. Said *Atlantic*. Said *no survivors expected*.

She didn't scream. She sat on the kitchen floor holding the pie tin to her chest like it was warm, like it was him at four, feverish, begging her to stay.

At 11:02 the phone rang. Unknown number.

"Mom?"

She couldn't breathe.

question: Where were you the day the last elephant died?
answer_raw:
My granddaughter asks it the way her teacher told her to, tablet held out, recording light blinking.

I want to tell her something worthy. That I wept. That I stood in a field.

The truth is I was repainting the bathroom. Seafoam, a color Denise picked and I hated. The radio was on, but the roller was loud, and I was on the ladder when the announcer said her name, Nandi, and something about Kenya, about seventy-one years, about the keepers singing.

I remember thinking, huh. That's a shame. I remember thinking I'd missed a spot by the vent.

Later there were documentaries, a stamp, a statue in every capital. People said they'd felt it, a shift in the air. I didn't feel anything. I finished the second coat and washed the brushes in the sink until the water ran clear.

"Grandpa?" she says. "You can say you don't remember."

But I do. That's the thing. I remember the exact color. I remember my shoulder aching. I remember how ordinary it was, how the world ended one piece at a time and none of us put down our rollers.

"I was home," I tell her. "I was busy."

She nods and writes it down, like it's an answer.

question: The zombie apocalypse finally happens! However, it only lasts about a month before the corpses are too rotted to move
answer_raw:
Gary had been ready for eleven years.

He had the bunker. He had the canned peaches, the water purification tablets, the crossbow he'd named Deborah. When the news broke that the dead were rising in Ohio, he felt something he hadn't felt since his wedding day: vindication.

He sealed the hatch and waited.

Week one, he watched through the periscope as they shambled past, gray and moaning. He took notes. He was magnificent.

Week two, they were slower. One of them lost an arm reaching for a mailbox and just stood there, confused.

Week three was August. Week three was bad. Gary could smell it through the filters.

By week four, the ones still moving were mostly sliding. A neighbor, Mr. Paulsen, formerly of the HOA, inched down the driveway on what remained of his torso, then simply stopped, like a phone at one percent.

On day thirty-three, Gary climbed out. The sun was bright. Birds were singing. Somewhere, a lawnmower started.

His wife was in the yard with a shovel and a face mask, helping the Hendersons bury Mr. Paulsen.

"Oh good," she said. "You're out. Grab a shovel."

"I had a crossbow," Gary said weakly.

"You had a crossbow," she agreed, and handed him the shovel.

question: Write a fable with a terrible moral of the story.
answer_raw:
**The Beaver Who Shared**

In a cold river lived a Beaver who had spent the whole summer building a lodge of sticks and mud. It was warm and dry, with a little shelf for storing bark.

When the first frost came, an Otter knocked at the door. "My den flooded," she said, shivering. "May I stay the winter?"

"Of course," said the Beaver, for his mother had taught him kindness.

The next week the Otter's cousins arrived, and then their cousins, and then a Muskrat who claimed to know somebody's cousin. Each one was cold, and each one was welcomed. They ate the bark on the little shelf. They ate the bark in the walls. One very large cousin ate the door.

By midwinter the lodge was so crowded that the Beaver slept outside on the ice, where he could hear his guests inside laughing about what a soft touch he was.

In spring the Otters left without a word. The Beaver, thin and frostbitten, began rebuilding. Across the river, a Wolverine who had never shared a crumb in his life lounged in a fat, snug den and watched him work.

*Moral: Kindness is a lovely trait to find in others.*

question: The United States of America finds itself in another civil war. You are a general of one of the sides in the middle of an interview. You just got finished answering a question about " politics ", and then the interviewer asks you, " What's the most brutal thing you've seen thus far in the war? "
answer_raw:
The general sets down his coffee. He studies the cup a long time, like the answer might be floating in it.

"You want a body count story. I've got those. Everybody's got those." He runs his thumb along the rim. "Harrisburg, second week. We took a subdivision off Route 22. Cul-de-sacs, basketball hoops, nice lawns. My boys went house to house, and in one kitchen there's a family eating dinner. Pot roast. They don't run. The father just points his fork at the window, across the street, and says, 'That's them. The Hendersons. They've got a flag in the garage.'"

He's quiet for a moment.

"We found the flag. We found the Hendersons. And the thing is, the father went back to eating. Asked his daughter to pass the rolls. I stood in that kitchen and understood he'd been waiting. Years, maybe. Through barbecues, carpools, Christmas cards. Waiting for somebody with a rifle to finally knock on his door so he could point."

He finishes the coffee.

"Artillery's brutal. But artillery doesn't know your name. That man knew their kids' birthdays. He'd probably been to the parties." He stands and buttons his jacket. "Next question. Something about logistics, please."

question: None of the angels knew the true purpose of their halos. Yours just broke.
answer_raw:
It cracked during the evening hymn, a hairline fracture, then a sound like a wineglass giving up.

The light went out of me all at once. I expected to fall. Instead I simply stood there in the choir, unlit, while ten thousand voices went on singing around me.

And I saw the Throne.

I had looked at it every day for eons. That was the point of looking: you could not see Him without being blinded by Him, and to be blinded was to be loved. But without my halo there was no glare. There was only a chair. Tall, gold, and empty, with dust gathered in the seams of the cushion.

Then I understood where the light came from.

Every halo in the choir was tilted toward the center. Ten thousand thin beams converged above the seat and braided themselves into a shape so bright it hurt. A face. A voice, humming in the overlap.

We were making Him. We had always been making Him.

Beside me, Seraphiel caught my eye, saw the dark ring above my head, and faltered mid-note.

"Keep singing," I whispered.

Because the light was weaker by one now, and I could see the face flickering, and I did not know what would happen if it went out.

question: Earth is a quarantined zone, holding the most deadly disease in the universe, H. Sapiens
answer_raw:
The probe reached the cordon on a Tuesday, by the natives' reckoning.

Warden Isk'thal had been dreading it for forty years. She watched it drift toward the boundary buoys: a tin can with a golden disc bolted to its side, broadcasting nothing, asking for everything.

"Incinerate?" asked her junior.

"Wait."

The first outbreak had been eleven thousand years ago. A survey team landed, stayed a season, and came home changed. They wept at sunsets. They named their children. One of them built a tower for no reason except that it was taller than the last one. Within a century the Concord's oldest species had invented war, and poetry, and the word *mine*.

So the Concord built the fence and kept the silence. They settled into the long patience of waiting for the infection to burn itself out.

It hadn't.

Isk'thal pulled the disc's contents onto her screen, against regulation. Whale song. A mother's first words to a newborn. Someone laughing.

Her chest did something it had never done before.

"Warden?"

She should have fired. She knew the protocols. Instead she found herself wondering what the laughing one had found so funny, and whether she might ever hear it again.

"Let it through," she said, and understood, too late, that she was already sick.

question: Fast food franchises have become the dominant religions. You meet some unsavoury acolytes of the Burger King whilst on a pilgrimage to Kentucky.
answer_raw:
The Colonel teaches that the road to Corbin is long, and that the faithful must walk it hungry. I had fasted since Ohio, eleven herbs and spices sewn into the hem of my robe, when the paper crowns appeared over the ridge.

There were four of them. Their leader wore his crown tilted, the way the zealots do, and his breath smelled of flame-broiling.

"Pilgrim," he said. "You look tired. You look like a man who's been told there's only one way."

"There is only one recipe," I said. "And it is secret."

His brothers laughed. One cracked his knuckles, and I saw the tattoo across them: HAVE IT YOUR WAY.

"That's the thing about secrets," the leader said. "Somebody always sells them." He held out a Whopper, still warm, glistening. "No mystery. No waiting. Just exactly what you want."

My stomach answered before I could.

"The Colonel makes you earn it," he whispered. "The King never makes you wait."

I thought of the white suit, the patient eyes on every bucket. I thought of Ohio.

I pulled the little bucket-shaped locket from my collar and held it up like a cross. "Original," I said. "Recipe."

They hissed and scattered into the treeline, crowns fluttering.

I walked on toward Kentucky, steadier, holier.

It was two miles before I noticed they'd taken my coupons.

question: High schools introduce " romantic relationships " as a new school subject. In order to pass, you have to find yourself a girlfriend/boyfriend before the end of the year.
answer_raw:
Mr. Delgado taped the syllabus to the whiteboard like a wanted poster. *Unit One: Eye Contact. Unit Four: Asking. Final Exam: Hold Hands at the Spring Formal, Witnessed.*

By March, most of the class had passed. Couples paraded to his desk for the stamp, fingers laced like they were carrying something fragile. Priya and Marcus got an A-plus for a promposal involving a drone. Tyler's relationship lasted six days, but the rubric didn't specify duration.

That left me and Wen Li, who sat by the window and drew birds in the margins of every worksheet.

"We could just do it," she said the week before formal, not looking up. "Hold hands. Get the stamp. Go back to normal."

"Sure," I said. "Efficient."

At the dance, the gym smelled like floor wax and fruit punch. Mr. Delgado stood by the bleachers with his clipboard. Wen Li's hand was cold, then less cold.

"Stamp," he said, and we got it.

Then we didn't let go, which was strange, because the assignment was over.

"Are we still doing the thing?" she asked.

"I think this is extra credit," I said.

She laughed, the real kind. And I realized I'd been failing a different class all year without knowing it existed.

question: A time traveler returns from the future, crying.
answer_raw:
Dr. Okafor stepped out of the chamber and folded onto the floor like a dropped coat.

We rushed her. Priya had the medkit open before anyone spoke. Marcus was already saying the word *contamination* into his radio, and I was bracing, honestly, for the sentence we'd all rehearsed in our nightmares: *It's gone. All of it.*

"It's fine," she said.

We waited for the rest.

"No, you don't understand. It's *fine*." She wiped her face with her sleeve and laughed, which was worse. "I went two hundred years out. There was a river where the old highway was. Kids swimming in it. A woman gave me a peach off a tree on a public street, just handed it to me, and when I told her where I came from she said, 'Oh, the hard years.' She said it so gently. Like I'd survived a fever."

Priya sat back on her heels. "Then why are you crying?"

Dr. Okafor looked at the chamber, then at the window, at the gray smear of our own sky, the sirens, the permits, the endless meetings where nothing moved.

"Because she thanked me," she said. "She thanked all of us. And we haven't done it yet."

Nobody said anything for a while.

Then Marcus put down the radio, and we went back to work.

question: Only a woman can make you feel guilty for doing something perfectly normal...
answer_raw:
I was eating a sandwich. That's all. Turkey on rye, standing at the kitchen counter at 12:40 on a Saturday, which is lunchtime by any reasonable measure.

She appeared in the doorway in her dinosaur pajamas, clutching a stuffed rabbit by one ear.

"You're eating," she said.

"I am."

"Without me."

"You had lunch an hour ago, bug. Mac and cheese. You threw the peas at the dog."

She considered this. Her lower lip began its slow, devastating journey outward.

"Buster ate the peas," she said, as if that settled something. "So I didn't really have lunch."

"That's not how it works."

She climbed onto the stool beside me, set the rabbit on the counter facing me like a witness, and folded her hands. She didn't ask. She just watched the sandwich. Then me. Then the sandwich.

I lasted maybe nine seconds.

"Half," I said.

"Mr. Flops wants some too."

"Mr. Flops is polyester."

She gave me the look her mother gives me when I claim the dishwasher's full enough to run. Four years old, and already perfected.

I made another sandwich. Triangles, crusts off. Mr. Flops got a corner.

Later, my wife asked why the turkey was gone.

"Don't," I said. "I've been through enough."

question: A story, a poem, a dialogue that makes people smile.

This is my first tooth. It is very good quality. I brushed it almost every day. I would like five dollars please, or a pony.
Love, Maya

Thank you for your excellent tooth. It is one of the finest I have collected this year. Sadly, ponies do not fit under pillows. I tried once. It was a whole thing. Enclosed please find two dollars and a glitter sticker.
Sparkles,
T. Fairy

Two dollars is okay. Why do you have my dad's handwriting?
Love, Maya

All grown-ups have fairy handwriting. It is a well-known fact. Please go to sleep.

You wrote "please go to sleep" exactly how Dad says it. Also you left your reading glasses on my dresser. And a cookie crumb.
Love, Maya
P.S. It's okay. I won't tell anybody. But I think the next tooth is worth three dollars.

**Dear Maya,**
Deal.
T. Fairy
P.S. Could I please have my glasses back? I can't find the other teeth without them.

question: Humans are not native to earth. After aliens defeated the human race, they banished captives to earth stripped of modern technology. Over time history became legend and legend forgotten. That is until in a mountain cave a mural drawing is found and an ancient metal object unlike ever seen before
answer_raw:
The cave had been sealed by a rockfall older than the valley's name. Mara squeezed through with her headlamp and forgot to breathe.

Painted in ochre and soot were people. Hundreds of them knelt in rows beneath tall figures with too many joints. Above them hung a sky with two suns. Then came a line of ships, sketched with a care no hunter had ever given a bison. Then a blue world. Then the people again, naked, walking into forest.

At the mural's end lay the object. It was gray and palm-sized, cold despite ten thousand years in the dark, with no corrosion and no seam. When her glove brushed it, the surface warmed, and a ring of light crawled across it like a waking eye.

Deshawn found her an hour later, sitting on the floor with the device in her lap.

"It spoke," she said.

"Mara..."

"Not words. It *showed* me. We weren't born here, Dee. We were dumped. They took everything: the tools, the language, the memory. They left us enough to survive and not enough to remember." She turned it over. A second ring lit, then a third. "It's a key. Someone hid it. Someone wanted us to find it."

"A key to what?"

Far above the atmosphere, something that had slept a very long time caught the signal and opened its eyes.

question: Write a story in which a character meets the author and tries to influence the outcome of the story
answer_raw:
The author was smaller than Marguerite expected, hunched at her kitchen table in a bathrobe, stirring coffee that had gone cold two drafts ago.

"You're not supposed to be in here," the author said.

"It's my kitchen." Marguerite sat down across from her. "I read ahead."

The author winced. "Chapter twelve."

"The storm. The rowboat. My brother's name on my lips as the water closes over." Marguerite folded her hands. "It's very pretty. I'd rather not."

"It's the whole point. Your death is what makes Tomas go home."

"Tomas is a grown man. He can take a bus."

The author laughed despite herself, then stopped. "Readers need it to cost something."

Marguerite looked at the author's hands: ink on one knuckle, a hospital bracelet she hadn't cut off yet. She looked at the second mug by the stove, the one nobody had used.

"Who drowned?" Marguerite asked gently.

The author didn't answer for a long time. Rain started against the window, the first gust of chapter twelve.

"Let it cost something else," Marguerite said. "Let it cost the boat."

The author picked up her pen. Outside, somewhere offshore, a rowboat slipped its rope and went out alone into the dark.

question: You're out for a jog when a man who looks just like you stumbles out of the bushes. He trusts a blood covered bag into your arms and whispers " break the cycle " before collapsing at your feet.
answer_raw:
Mile four, where the path bends along the creek, he came out of the laurels like something thrown.

He had my face. My jaw, my crooked left eyebrow, older by maybe a week without sleep. He shoved a canvas bag into my chest, wet and warm, and his breath hit my ear.

"Break the cycle."

Then his knees went. He folded onto the gravel and did not get up.

I should have called someone. Instead I opened the bag.

Inside was my running watch, cracked. A kitchen knife from my own block, the one with the chipped handle. And a notebook in my handwriting, pages of tally marks, each row ending in the same note: *Told him. He opened the bag.*

The last page said: *Don't read this. Throw it in the creek and go home. She's still alive at 7:40.*

My watch said 7:31.

I looked at him, at the blood that wasn't all his, at the knife I hadn't used yet.

Footsteps crunched on the path behind me. Someone called my name, and I knew the voice. I'd know it anywhere.

I threw the bag into the creek.

Then I sat down in the gravel beside my own body, closed my eyes, and waited to find out what kind of man I was without it.

question: A young man, with no helmet on, riding a motorcycle down a mountain road on an overcast day.
answer_raw:
The helmet was still on the hook by his mother's door, and Danny knew it. He'd seen it on the way out, the scuffed black shell she'd bought him for his nineteenth birthday, and he'd walked past it the way you walk past someone you're not speaking to.

The clouds sat low on Harlan Ridge, so low the road seemed to run into them and not come out. Wind came up off the valley cold and wet and filled his mouth when he breathed. His eyes watered. He let them.

He took the first switchback slower than he meant to, the second one faster. By the fourth the old Honda was leaning so far the footpeg kissed asphalt with a small, bright scream, and something in his chest answered it.

Nobody had told him grief could feel like this. It wasn't heavy. It was light, dangerously light, as if the whole mountain had let go of him.

At the overlook he pulled over and killed the engine. Below, the town was a gray smudge, his father's shop somewhere inside it with the lights off.

He sat until his hands stopped shaking.

Then he turned around, rode back up slow, and went in for the helmet.

question: Through what he describes as a series of " entirely involuntary " and " incredibly unfortunate " events, Ron Swanson is elected President of The United States of America.
answer_raw:
The first unfortunate event was Leslie Knope filing his candidacy paperwork while he was on a fishing trip without cell reception, as God intended.

The second was a debate moderator asking what he would do about the national deficit. Ron said, "Nothing. I would sit in the Oval Office and do nothing, and the government would shrink out of pure neglect, like a houseplant." The clip was viewed four hundred million times.

The third was his opponent calling him "a mustache with no platform." Ron replied that a mustache was a platform, and that it had supported more meaningful things than his opponent ever had. Ohio went red, then blue, then a color scientists are still classifying.

Now he sat behind the Resolute Desk, which he had to admit was fine craftsmanship. Oak. Honest joinery.

"Sir," said an aide, "your first executive order?"

Ron considered it. He lifted a pen. He wrote: *All federal employees may go home.*

"For the day, sir?"

"For as long as they like."

The aide hesitated. "And you, Mr. President?"

Ron leaned back and folded his hands over a plate of bacon that had materialized, as bacon does, when needed most.

"I'm going to build a canoe," he said, "and I'm going to do it on the South Lawn, and no one is going to stop me. That is my first act of freedom."

question: Humanity is on the losing side of war. Battle training is part of school curriculum, and the world wide military enlistment age has been lowered to 14. Tomorrow is your 14th birthday.
answer_raw:
Mom made the cake tonight instead of tomorrow. She said the oven's been acting up, but we both know the bus comes at six.

It's lemon, my favorite, with frosting she stretched out of powdered milk and the last of the sugar ration. She wrote my name on it in blue. The candles are old ones from Danny's box, burned down to stubs. Fourteen stubs. He only got to use them once.

In drill class today, Sergeant Okafor made us field-strip rifles blindfolded. I finished in forty seconds. She said I had good hands. I used to think that meant piano.

Dad isn't talking. He's been fixing the same radio for three hours, turning one screw in and out, in and out.

After cake, Mom sat on my bed and braided my hair tight against my scalp, the way they tell you so it won't catch. Her fingers shook. I pretended not to notice, and she pretended I wasn't pretending.

"Make a wish," she'd said earlier, and I did. I wished the war would end before six.

The clock says 11:52.

I'm going to close my eyes now, before it changes. If I don't see midnight, maybe it doesn't count.

question: The year is 2200 an alien race has come to earth revealing that the human race was nothing but an experiment by their ancestors.
answer_raw:
The ship didn't land so much as settle, the way a cat settles onto a warm windowsill it has always considered its own.

The Veth were tall and apologetic. Their spokesperson, Oru, stood before the General Assembly in Geneva with a slab of something that wasn't quite stone and wasn't quite glass.

"Our ancestors made you," Oru said. The translation hummed through four hundred languages at once. "Seeded the planet. Nudged the chemistry. Stepped away to observe."

The chamber erupted. Priests wept. Physicists laughed too loudly. Someone threw a shoe.

Secretary-General Amara Delacroix waited for the noise to thin. "Why?" she asked. "What was the experiment?"

Oru's face did something complicated. "That is why we came."

It set the slab on the podium. Light bloomed across its surface: star charts, genetic sequences, ten thousand years of careful notes in a script no one alive could fully read.

"The final entry is missing," Oru said. "Our ancestors left before recording the hypothesis. We do not know what they hoped you would become. We do not know what result they were waiting for."

The silence stretched across the whole planet.

"So you came to ask us," Delacroix said slowly.

Oru bowed its long head. "We came to ask you. Did it work?"
